excerpt: Silk, formerly Kaminario, sells a software-defined cloud data platform that speeds up databases and cuts storage costs on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. History, funding and alternatives.
content:
Silk is a cloud storage and data platform company. Its software sits between a public cloud's infrastructure and a customer's databases and applications, and its website pitches it as a cloud data platform for the AI era that runs input/output-heavy applications up to ten times faster at up to 70% lower cost. It works on Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. The site lists use cases including AI inference, predictable application performance, managing database copies for development and testing, and controlling cloud costs, and it targets database administrators and analytics teams.

Silk has a long history under another name. Blocks and Files reported that it began as Kaminario, founded in 2008 as an all-flash storage array vendor, which later became a software-defined storage company and then a cloud database accelerator. Kaminario renamed itself Silk in July 2020. (A Silk spokesperson told the publication that Silk itself dates from 2019.) The CEO is Dani Golan, described in the funding announcement as founder and CEO.

In July 2021 Silk raised $55 million, led by S Capital, with existing investors Sequoia Capital, Pitango, Globespan, Ibex and Vintage, and new investors including Clal Insurance, Bank Hapoalim, Meitav Dash and Menora Mivtachim. Blocks and Files put total funding at $313 million for the combined Kaminario and Silk entity, or $90 million for Silk alone.

Customers shown on Silk's site include Sentara Health, Wayfair, eToro, HealthEquity, Franciscan Health and SimCorp. The company cites customer results such as $2.8 million in annual storage savings at Franciscan and 32 times faster analytics at Sentara Health; these are the company's own figures. Silk does not list prices on its website; its packaging is sized to each workload, and buyers contact sales.

This page is research, not a review. We have not tested Silk; facts come from its website and the reporting under Sources.

use_cases: Speeding up I/O-heavy databases running in the public cloud
Reducing cloud storage costs for large databases
Creating database copies for development, testing and analytics
Keeping application performance predictable during cloud migration
Feeding data to AI inference workloads

fit: enterprises running large, performance-sensitive databases in AWS, Azure or Google Cloud
DBA teams that need fast database copies
healthcare, financial services and retail companies, which Silk targets
not_fit: small apps whose cloud provider's standard storage is already fast enough
buyers who want transparent list prices

pricing.intro: Silk's website describes packaging that scales with workloads but does not list prices. Buyers contact sales for a quote.

pros: Works across the three major public clouds
No changes needed to the database or application, the company says
Large enterprise customers in healthcare and finance
cons: Performance and savings figures are vendor claims

alternatives.intro: Other ways to run high-performance database storage in the cloud.

items.name: NetApp Cloud Volumes ONTAP
items.what: NetApp's storage software running in public clouds
items.difference: Mature enterprise storage features from a long-time vendor.

items.name: Pure Storage Cloud Block Store
items.what: Pure Storage's block storage software for AWS and Azure
items.difference: Extends Pure's on-premises arrays into the cloud.

items.name: Lightbits Labs
items.difference: Focuses on high-performance NVMe over TCP.

faq.a: Yes. Kaminario renamed itself Silk in July 2020, Blocks and Files reported.
